title: Inflation: the RBI cannot grow onions
hook:
In July 2023, customers at McDonald's outlets in Delhi found a small notice at the counter: despite best efforts, the chain could not get enough tomatoes that passed its quality checks, so burgers would come without them for a while. Tomato prices had gone vertical after a lean season and monsoon chaos on the roads. Vegetable vendors in Mumbai said customers had simply stopped buying. That month's inflation print jumped to its highest in over a year.

And the RBI? It did nothing. No hike, no emergency meeting, barely a raised eyebrow.

Fast forward to October 2026. Inflation was running at a level that looked, on paper, perfectly manageable. Fuel prices had not even fully reached the index yet. And the RBI raised rates anyway.

So which is it? Does the RBI care about inflation or not? The answer is that it cares about a very specific kind of inflation, and to see which kind, you have to open up the basket and look at what is inside. That is what this chapter does.
short: India's inflation basket is dominated by two things monetary policy cannot touch: food, which swings with the monsoon, and fuel, whose pump price is set by the government and the state oil companies rather than by the market.
Food is the noise, core is the signal. The MPC looks through food spikes it judges temporary and moves when they leak into core prices and household expectations.

An oil shock reaches the index late and in jumps, because pump prices follow excise decisions and oil company losses, not Brent in real time. Part of the shock is absorbed by the government before you ever see it.

The rule is forward-looking: a four percent target with a band of two points either side, acted on through the forecast several quarters out, with one eye on the rupee. That is why October's hike came before fuel reached the index.
For stocks, the question is never just whether the print is high. It is whether the pressure is broadening, because broadening into core is what turns one hike into a cycle.

sections.heading: What is actually in the basket, and why that decides everything
sections.html:
Start with what the number is. The consumer price index, or CPI, measures each month what a typical household pays for a fixed shopping list, with prices collected across towns and villages and each item weighted by its share of the household budget. Inflation is simply how much that weighted shopping list costs now compared with the same month a year ago.

Here's the thing that makes India different. The weights come from surveys of what Indians actually spend on, and Indians spend a big chunk of their money on food. In the series the RBI targeted for most of the last decade, food and drinks made up nearly half the basket. In a rich country, rent, healthcare and services dominate instead.

That changed somewhat in early 2026, when the statistics ministry launched a new series built on a fresh household spending survey, with 2024 as its base year. Food's weight dropped to a little over a third and the basket was split into twelve groups instead of six. That should make headline inflation less jumpy. But a third is still a lot. A bad onion season can still move the national number.

Inside the basket, it is worth knowing the main families:

  • Cereals like rice and wheat, whose prices are heavily managed by the government through minimum support prices, procurement by the Food Corporation of India and occasional export bans.
  • Vegetables, the wild child. Tomatoes, onions and potatoes are perishable, seasonal and grown in a handful of states, so a single bad week of rain can double their price.
  • Pulses and edible oils, which India imports in large quantities, so they carry global prices and the rupee into your kitchen.
  • Everything else, from milk and rent to tuition, which moves far more slowly.

One subtlety trips up even seasoned readers. The petrol and diesel you put in your car do not sit in the fuel group. They sit under transport. The fuel group is mostly about cooking gas, kerosene and electricity. So when a headline says fuel inflation is low, it may say very little about what is happening at the petrol pump.

sections.heading: Food inflation is a weather report, not a demand signal
sections.html:
Why does food matter so much to how the RBI thinks? Because most of the swings in Indian food prices have nothing to do with how much money is chasing goods. They are about supply.

Think about how a tomato gets to your plate. It is grown in a few belts, mostly by small farmers, harvested within a narrow window and has to reach a city market within days before it rots. If the monsoon arrives late, sowing is delayed. If unseasonal rain lashes Maharashtra and Karnataka at harvest time, crops are ruined in the field. If a heatwave hits in spring, yields shrink. Each is a supply shock: the same buyers chasing fewer tomatoes.

Then there is the farmer's own response, which economists call the cobweb cycle. When tomato prices are sky high this season, farmers rush to plant more tomatoes next season. Next season there is a glut, prices crash and farmers dump produce on highways. So they plant less, and the cycle restarts. Vegetable inflation in India often looks like a saw blade for exactly this reason.

Edible oil and pulses add a global twist. India imports much of its cooking oil, palm from Indonesia and Malaysia, sunflower from the Black Sea. A war or an export ban there reaches Indian kitchens within weeks.

A rate hike does not make it rain. It just makes everything else more expensive to borrow for while the onions stay dear.

So here is the MPC's logic. Rate hikes work by cooling demand: fewer home loans, car purchases and business borrowing. That does nothing for a rain-made tomato shortage. Hiking would squeeze the whole economy while food prices sort themselves out within a few months anyway. So when the committee judges a food shock to be temporary, it looks through it. The phrase you will see in the statements is that it will look through first-round effects.

The catch is the word temporary. Which brings us to the number the RBI actually watches.

sections.heading: Headline is the noise, core is the signal
sections.html:
Strip food and fuel out of the basket and what remains is called core inflation. It covers things like clothing, household goods, personal care, medicines, tuition, haircuts and restaurant meals. These prices are set by businesses that look at their costs, their wage bills and how many customers are walking in. In other words, they respond to demand and to expectations, which is precisely what interest rates can influence.

Why does core matter so much? Because it is where a temporary food shock becomes a permanent problem. Economists call this second-round effects, and it works step by step.

  • Food prices stay high for several months.
  • Workers whose grocery bills have jumped ask for higher wages, and domestic help, drivers and factory workers get raises.
  • Restaurants, salons and small manufacturers pass those wage costs on in their own prices.
  • Households start to assume prices will keep rising, so they spend earlier and bargain harder, which makes it self-fulfilling.

Once inflation is baked into wages and expectations, it no longer goes away when the monsoon recovers. That is the moment the RBI stops looking through and starts acting.

To keep an eye on that last step, the RBI runs a regular survey asking households in major cities what inflation they expect. Households routinely expect inflation far higher than the official print, so the committee watches the direction of the answers more than their level.

One more tool for reading the monthly number: base effects. Because inflation compares today's prices with a year ago, an odd month last year can distort this year's print. If vegetable prices crashed twelve months ago, this month's inflation will look high even if prices have been flat for weeks. Analysts always ask how much of a move is genuine new pressure and how much is the calendar playing tricks.

sections.heading: Why an oil shock arrives late and in lumps
sections.html:
In theory, petrol prices were freed from government control in 2010 and diesel in 2014. In practice, the three state oil marketing companies, Indian Oil, Bharat Petroleum and Hindustan Petroleum, run most of the country's petrol pumps, and they do not change prices every time Brent crude moves. They often hold prices steady for months and then move in a series of steps.

Why sell fuel below cost? Because the pump price is a political number and the government owns most of these companies. When crude spikes and retail prices are frozen, they sell at a loss. Those losses are called under-recoveries. They are, in effect, a subsidy paid by the oil companies' shareholders on the government's behalf, which is why economists call them quasi-fiscal: a cost to the state that never shows up in the budget.

Then there is tax. A big slice of what you pay at the pump is central excise duty and state VAT. That gives the government a shock absorber. In May 2022, the finance ministry cut excise to cushion the war spike. In March 2026, as the Iran war sent crude above a hundred dollars, it cut excise sharply again to reduce the oil companies' losses. Only from May 2026 did the companies start raising pump prices in rounds.

Follow the chain and you see why an oil shock hits the CPI late:

  • Day one: crude jumps. Nothing happens at the pump.
  • Weeks later: the government trims excise and the oil companies absorb losses. Still little in the index.
  • Months later: pump prices rise in steps, and the direct effect lands in the transport group.
  • After that: the indirect effects creep in. Truck freight rises, so vegetables cost more to move. Fertiliser, plastics, paint and packaging get dearer. Airlines raise fares.

A weak rupee piles on top of all this, because crude, edible oil, gold and electronics are priced in dollars. When the rupee slides, all of those get dearer in rupee terms even if their dollar price stays still. That is imported inflation, and it is the reason the RBI cannot treat the currency as somebody else's problem.

sections.heading: What the RBI actually reacts to
sections.html:
Since 2016, the RBI has worked under what is called flexible inflation targeting. The government, in consultation with the RBI, sets a target for CPI inflation of four percent, with a tolerance band of two points either side, for five years at a time. The six-member Monetary Policy Committee is legally bound to aim for it. If inflation stays outside the band for three quarters in a row, the committee has failed, and it must write to the government explaining why, what it will do about it and how long it will take.

The word flexible matters: the committee also keeps growth in mind, which is why it can look through food shocks.

The other thing that matters is time. Rate changes take several quarters to work through loans, spending and prices. So the committee steers not by today's print but by its own forecast a year or so ahead, the way a driver watches the road, not the mirror. If that forecast sits above target, it tightens, even if today's number looks fine.

[[fig:1]]

The chart shows headline CPI inflation month by month against the dashed four percent line. Notice the gap in 2025: that is the switch to the new series, and because the old and new indices do not overlap in our feed, year-on-year inflation simply cannot be computed for most of that year. On the right, look at the direction rather than the level. Through 2026 the line climbs steadily back above the target, and fuel has not yet fully arrived.

Put those pieces together and October 2026 makes sense. Inflation was not alarming yet. But the committee could see the whole pipeline: crude up sharply, pump prices set to rise, the rupee under pressure and its own forecast drifting higher. Hiking before fuel reached the index was the forward-looking rule doing exactly what it was designed to do. Waiting for the print would have meant acting too late.

So the honest summary of the RBI's reaction function is this. It ignores food spikes it thinks will pass. It reacts to anything that threatens to broaden into core or lift expectations. And it gives real weight to the rupee, because a falling currency is inflation that has not shown up yet.

sections.heading: Where inflation hits your portfolio
sections.html:
Inflation is not one shock to the stock market. It is several, travelling through different pipes.

The consumer's wallet. Food takes a much bigger bite out of a poorer household's budget than a richer one's. When food inflation runs hot, lower-income and rural families cut back on everything else first: soap, biscuits, two-wheelers, a new phone. Consumer staples companies see volumes slow, often with a lag of a couple of quarters.

The input bill. Staples companies buy palm oil, wheat, milk, sugar and plastic packaging, much of it linked to global commodities and crude. When those costs rise faster than they can raise prices, margins get squeezed. The first line of defence is a quiet one: the pack stays at the same price but has fewer biscuits in it. Shrinkflation buys time, but not much.

The saver's choice. When bank deposits pay less than inflation, savers look elsewhere: gold and property in the late 2000s, equity funds once real rates turned positive. The flood of money into Indian equities after 2016 owes a lot to lower, steadier inflation.

The valuation multiple. Higher inflation means higher interest rates and bond yields, and that lowers the value of profits far in the future. Expensive growth stocks feel it most.

The winners. Companies with pricing power, those that can raise prices without losing customers, along with commodity producers whose output price is the thing rising, tend to hold up best.

history_title: onions, tomatoes and a letter nobody saw

history.title: The years India bought gold instead of shares
history.story:
After the drought of 2009 and the big stimulus that followed the global financial crisis, food inflation in India ran in double digits for long stretches. Governor D. Subbarao raised rates again and again, but bank deposits still paid less than inflation. Savers were losing money in the bank, so they did what Indian households always do when they distrust the rupee: they bought gold and property.

Gold imports, paid in dollars, helped push the current account deficit to a record. In 2013 Finance Minister P. Chidambaram raised the gold import duty three times in one year, and smuggling boomed, just as he had warned it would. That same summer the rupee went into free fall in the taper tantrum.
history.lesson: Persistent inflation does not just hurt prices, it pulls household savings out of the financial system, and that is bad for equities for years.

history.title: Writing a number on the wall
history.story:
When Raghuram Rajan took over the RBI in September 2013, one of his first moves was to set up a committee under Deputy Governor Urjit Patel to rethink how monetary policy worked. Its report, in January 2014, recommended that the RBI target CPI inflation, aim for four percent with a band around it, glide down to it from the double digits, and hand rate decisions to a committee. Markets read it as hawkish.

The government and the RBI signed a framework agreement in 2015, Parliament wrote it into the RBI Act in 2016, and the first Monetary Policy Committee met that October, with Patel now governor. Within a few years, inflation and inflation expectations had come down sharply.
history.lesson: A credible target changes behaviour. Once people believe the number, wages and prices start to bend toward it.

history.title: The onion that froze a cutting cycle
history.story:
Onions have a long history of embarrassing Indian governments; high onion prices were widely blamed for the ruling party's defeat in the Delhi election of 1998. In late 2019 they struck again. Unseasonal rains in October and November ruined crops, exports were banned and state traders scrambled to import onions from as far away as Egypt and Turkey.

The MPC had cut rates five times that year to revive a slowing economy, and markets expected a sixth in December. Instead, with food prices surging, Governor Shaktikanta Das held rates, surprising almost everyone. Weeks later headline inflation jumped above the upper end of the band, its highest since 2014. Still the committee did not hike: excluding onions, inflation was comfortably inside the band, and the onions duly came back down.
history.lesson: A food spike can pause a cutting cycle, but on its own it rarely starts a hiking one.

history.title: Everything, everywhere, all at once
history.story:
Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 hit India's kitchen from three sides. Ukraine was a giant supplier of sunflower oil. In April, Indonesia banned palm oil exports. In May, a brutal heatwave shrank the wheat crop and India banned wheat exports. Meanwhile crude spiked. This was food and fuel, local and global, all at once.

Das moved between meetings with a surprise hike in May, and Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman cut fuel excise weeks later. It still was not enough to stop inflation staying above the band for three quarters in a row. In November 2022, for the first time ever, the MPC met in a special session to draft a letter to the government explaining its failure. The letter was submitted and never made public.
history.lesson: When food and fuel spike together, the RBI acts fast, because that is exactly the combination that leaks into core.

history.title: When McDonald's dropped the tomato
history.story:
In the summer of 2023, wholesale tomato prices in some markets nearly quadrupled in a month. McDonald's outlets in north and east India took tomatoes off the menu, and the government ordered its cooperative agencies to buy tomatoes in the producing states and sell them cheap in Delhi. Headline inflation shot up to its highest in over a year.

The MPC held rates and said, in effect, that it would wait. By the autumn, a flood of fresh planting had sent tomato prices crashing, exactly as the cobweb cycle predicts, and headline inflation fell back.
history.lesson: Vegetable spikes come and go within a season. Do not trade the headline, trade the core.

history.title: The elephant that went for a walk
history.story:
In April 2024, Das gave the market a line it still quotes. Inflation, he said, had been the elephant in the room two years earlier; now it had gone out for a walk and appeared to be returning to the forest. The elephant kept walking: inflation fell to multi-year lows, and Das's successor Sanjay Malhotra cut rates repeatedly through 2025.

Then the Iran war broke out in early 2026 and crude surged. The government cut excise, the oil companies swallowed losses, and pump prices rose only in steps. Headline inflation began climbing from its lows. In October 2026, with the rupee under pressure and fuel still on its way into the index, the RBI hiked.
history.lesson: Low starting inflation buys time, but not against an oil shock that is also a currency shock.

today:
Inflation is at [[val:cpi]], up [[val:cpi_3m]] in three months. Underneath, food is running hotter than the headline while the housing and fuel group is still well below it, which tells you the oil shock has not fully arrived. Brent is at [[val:brent]], up [[val:brent_3m]] in three months, and the rupee is at [[val:usdinr]] per dollar. The RBI's stance as we last set it: [[val:rbi]].

Expect the next couple of prints to rise as pump prices and freight costs catch up; a hiking RBI has already partly priced that. The real question is broadening. Watch three things: core inflation in the official release, the RBI's household expectations survey, and whether the oil companies keep pump prices frozen or pass more of the crude bill on. A late or weak monsoon on top of the oil shock would be the worst combination.
sowhat:
In an oil-led inflation turn with a hiking RBI, the pressure lands unevenly.

  • Prefer businesses with pricing power and low commodity input costs, and producers whose selling price is the thing that is rising.
  • Be careful with consumer staples: input costs rise before price hikes stick, and rural volumes slow when food eats the household budget.
  • Be careful with discretionary consumption aimed at lower-income buyers, such as entry-level two-wheelers and mass consumer durables.
  • Long-duration growth stocks on rich valuations suffer as yields rise with inflation expectations.
  • Watch the oil marketing companies: when prices are frozen, their shareholders are paying the subsidy.

What would flip it: core staying soft while headline rises, crude easing, and the RBI's language shifting back toward looking through.
